text: You've seen the question-mark placeholder show up in every lesson so far. This is the lesson where you learn exactly why it matters -- and what goes wrong in real code when you skip it.

This looks completely fine with a clean value like Trail Runner GTX. But the moment product_name comes from a user, a web form, or a file you don't fully control, building the query with an f-string becomes a real liability.

Watch what happens if that value arrives as this instead. Spliced into the f-string, SQL Server doesn't see one query anymore -- it sees two statements: the harmless select, and a second one that drops the entire Product table. That's SQL injection.

The fix is the question-mark placeholder you've already been using. product_name gets sent to SQL Server as a value, never as part of the SQL text. Even that malicious string would just fail to match any product name -- it literally cannot be interpreted as SQL.
Placeholders aren't limited to one value. Multiple question marks take multiple values, filled in order -- here, a start date and an end date for a BETWEEN clause.

And it's not only about security -- a name like O'Brien's Gear breaks a hand-built query string because the apostrophe ends the quoted literal early, but it's handled correctly as a parameter every time. The rule has no real exceptions: anything that isn't a literal you typed yourself belongs in a parameter.
Next lesson brings in SQLAlchemy, a toolkit that sits on top of pyodbc and gives pandas a more consistent way to read and write against the database.
